title: Metabolism
in30Seconds: Metabolism is the name for all the physical and chemical processes in the body that convert or use energy. Breathing, circulating blood, controlling body temperature, contracting muscles, digesting food, removing waste, and running the brain and nerves are all metabolic work. Two kinds of reactions do the job: anabolism builds and stores, catabolism breaks things down to release energy. Metabolic rate is how fast the body uses energy, and basal metabolism is the resting baseline. It changes with age, body size and muscle, and activity. Food supplies the fuel and building blocks that keep it all going.
whyItMatters: Every bite of food eventually meets metabolism, the chemical engine that turns nutrients into energy and building materials. Knowing how that engine works matters because it explains why the same body can need fuel for thinking, warming up, and healing, not just for moving. It also inoculates against a familiar myth: metabolism is not a switch that special foods can flip on. It is steady, round-the-clock work that shifts gradually with age and body composition. Seeing it that way makes talk about calories, energy, and food far easier to follow, and the topics that cover those details build directly on this picture.
learningObjectives: Define metabolism as the full set of physical and chemical processes in the body that convert or use energy, and name everyday processes it covers (breathing, circulation, temperature control, muscle contraction, digestion, waste removal, brain and nerve function).
Distinguish anabolism, the building-and-storing side of metabolism, from catabolism, the breaking-down side that releases energy, and give an original example of each.
Explain what metabolic rate is, state what basal metabolic rate measures, and describe how age, body size and composition, muscle, and activity influence it.
Trace how food connects to metabolism: digestion releases glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids that cells use as energy or store for later.
Apply the honest framing: metabolism is continuous steady work that changes gradually, not a switch that foods or habits can instantly turn up or down.

collegeVersion.heading: Metabolism: the body's chemical work
collegeVersion.body:
Metabolism is the name for all the physical and chemical processes in the body that convert or use energy. The U.S. National Library of Medicine's MedlinePlus defines it exactly that way, and lists what that work looks like in ordinary life: breathing, circulating blood, controlling body temperature, contracting muscles, digesting food and nutrients, eliminating waste through urine and feces, and the functioning of the brain and nerves. In other words, metabolism is not one thing that happens in one organ. It is the running total of chemical activity that keeps a person alive from moment to moment.

That activity is organized and sped up by enzymes, proteins that control specific chemical reactions in the cells. Thousands of these reactions occur at the same time, all coordinated by the body, to keep cells healthy and working. When people call metabolism the body's engine, they are pointing at this continuous chemical work: fuel in, energy out, heat produced, waste removed.

collegeVersion.heading: Anabolism and catabolism: build and break
collegeVersion.body:
Metabolic reactions come in two broad kinds, and they run at the same time. Anabolism is the building and storing side. It uses small building blocks, such as amino acids from digested protein, and assembles them into larger, more complex molecules the body needs, such as new muscle protein. It also stores energy for later, for example by packing glucose into a stored form in the liver and muscles. Catabolism is the breaking-down side. It takes large molecules, mostly carbohydrates and fats, and splits them apart to release energy. That released energy fuels anabolism, warms the body, and lets muscles contract. The breakdown also produces waste products, which leave the body through the skin, kidneys, lungs, and intestines.

A simple way to keep the pair straight: anabolism builds up and stores, catabolism breaks down and releases. After a meal, the balance tilts toward anabolism, because fresh fuel has just arrived and the body is in restock-and-repair mode.

collegeVersion.heading: Metabolic rate and basal metabolism
collegeVersion.body:
Metabolic rate is simply how fast the body uses energy. Because bodies differ, so do rates. The resting baseline is called the basal metabolic rate, or BMR: a measure of how quickly the body burns energy while at rest, keeping the heart beating, the lungs filling, and the body warm. Even asleep, the body is doing metabolic work, and BMR is the pace of that idle work.

Several things influence that pace, and they are worth naming factually. Age matters: metabolism generally slows with age, in part because muscle mass tends to decrease over the years, and muscle burns more energy at rest than fat does. Body composition matters: people with more muscle and less fat generally have higher resting rates, because muscle tissue is more demanding than fat tissue at rest. Body size matters too, larger bodies have more tissue doing work. Activity matters: moving and exercising raise energy use well above the resting baseline. Genes also play a role. None of this is advice about weight; it is simply what determines how fast different bodies use energy.

collegeVersion.heading: Food: the fuel and the building blocks
collegeVersion.body: Metabolism runs on what food provides. After a person eats, the digestive system breaks nutrients down into simpler forms: carbohydrates become simple sugars such as glucose, proteins become amino acids, and fats become fatty acids. The blood absorbs these molecules and carries them to the cells. Inside the cells, enzymes take over, and the body decides what to do with the delivery: use it as energy right away, or store it for later in tissues such as the liver, the muscles, and body fat. In this sense food is both fuel and building material. The energy side, how much energy each food carries and how the body tracks it, belongs to the topic on energy and calories. The building side shows up every time the body repairs tissue, grows, or replaces worn-out cells.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest picture: steady work, not a switch
collegeVersion.body: The most important thing to understand about metabolism may be what it is not. It is not a switch that can be flipped on by a spicy drink, a special herb, or a miracle food, and it does not simply switch off when a person sits still. Metabolism is steady work, running at some pace every second of every day, and shifting gradually in response to real, slow-moving factors such as age and body composition. Claims that a product can dramatically 'boost' or 'reset' metabolism should be read with suspicion; the honest picture is less dramatic and more impressive: an engine that never stops, adjusts its idle speed over a lifetime, and depends on food for both its fuel and its building materials.

vocabulary.definition: All the physical and chemical processes in the body that convert or use energy, from breathing and circulating blood to digesting food and powering the brain.
The building and storing side of metabolism, in which the body assembles small molecules into larger ones, such as turning amino acids into muscle protein.
The breaking-down side of metabolism, in which the body splits large molecules apart to release energy and produces waste products along the way.
A protein that speeds up and controls a specific chemical reaction in the body; enzymes carry out the reactions of metabolism.
How fast the body uses energy overall, combining the energy spent at rest with the energy spent on movement and activity.
A measure of how quickly the body burns energy while at rest, keeping basic functions such as heartbeat, breathing, and temperature running.
A simple sugar produced when carbohydrates are digested; it is a main fuel that cells can use for energy.
A substance in food, such as a carbohydrate, protein, or fat, that the body can use for energy, building materials, or both.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Metabolism is the body's engine. It is the sum of every chemical process that keeps you running, from breathing and pumping blood to digesting food and thinking. The engine does two kinds of jobs at once. One crew builds: it takes small pieces from food, like amino acids, and snaps them together into bigger things your body needs, such as muscle. That building work is anabolism. Another crew demolishes: it takes big molecules apart to release energy for the engine, and the leftovers become waste. That breaking-down work is catabolism. The engine also has a speed: metabolic rate is how fast your body uses energy. Basal metabolism is the idle speed, the energy burned just to keep your heart beating and your lungs filling while you rest.
eli10.analogy: Picture a city that never sleeps. Food is the fuel delivery, and the power plant burns it to keep the lights on across the whole city. Construction crews raise new buildings from stacks of bricks, which is anabolism. Wrecking crews tear down old buildings and turn them into usable scrap and rubble, which is catabolism. The plant hums along at an idle pace even at 3 a.m., when almost everyone sleeps, and that idle pace is the city's basal metabolism. A bigger city with more working crews, more buildings, and more fuel trucks runs hotter than a small one.
eli10.analogyLimits: A power plant can be shut down for maintenance, but the body's metabolism never switches off completely, it keeps working even during deep sleep. The analogy also makes building and demolition look like separate teams with separate sites, while in the body both kinds of reactions run side by side inside nearly every cell, all the time.

workedExample: Think through one ordinary afternoon with a student named Priya. At 2 p.m. she is sitting in class, but her body is still doing heavy chemical work: her lungs draw air, her heart pushes blood, and her brain burns energy to follow the lecture, all examples of metabolism in action. At 4 p.m. she jogs two miles; her contracting leg muscles need extra energy, so her cells break down stored fuel faster, a burst of catabolism, while her rising body temperature triggers cooling. At 6 p.m. she eats rice, chicken, and broccoli. Digestion breaks the rice into glucose, the chicken into amino acids, and the oil in the sauce into fatty acids. The blood carries these to her cells: some molecules are burned for energy right away, some amino acids are assembled into protein to repair the jogged muscles, anabolism at work, and the rest is stored for later. None of this stops when she falls asleep; it simply settles back to the basal pace.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking metabolism is only about weight gain and weight loss.
commonMistakes.correction: Metabolism covers every physical and chemical process that converts or uses energy, including breathing, circulation, temperature control, digestion, and brain function. Weight is only one small window onto it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing a special food or drink can switch metabolism on or off.
commonMistakes.correction: Metabolism is continuous steady work. It changes gradually with things like age and body composition, but no single food flips it like a light switch.
Anabolism builds and stores, using small pieces to make bigger molecules. Catabolism breaks big molecules down and releases energy in the process.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming metabolic rate is fixed at birth and never changes.
commonMistakes.correction: Metabolic rate shifts over a lifetime. It generally slows with age, partly because muscle mass tends to decrease, and muscle burns more energy at rest than fat does.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking only muscles use the energy from food.
commonMistakes.correction: Every cell uses fuel. Digested sugars, amino acids, and fatty acids travel in the blood to cells throughout the body, which use them for energy or store them, especially in the liver, muscles, and fat tissue.

compareContrast.distinction: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller building blocks and stores energy for later, while catabolism breaks large molecules apart and releases energy, also producing waste.
Metabolic rate is how fast the body uses energy overall, while basal metabolic rate is the resting baseline, the energy used at complete rest to keep basic functions going.

keyTakeaway: Metabolism is the body's steady chemical work: it converts and uses energy for everything from breathing to thinking, builds and stores with anabolism, breaks down for energy with catabolism, and runs at a pace set by age, body composition, and activity. It is not a switch, and food is the fuel and building material that keeps it going.

questionBank.prompt: A health teacher asks students to point to everyday examples of metabolism, the body's chemical work. Which list is entirely made of processes that fit the standard definition?
options: Breathing, circulating blood, digesting food
Sleeping, dreaming, waking up
Shopping, cooking, cleaning
Laughing, clapping, waving
questionBank.explanation: MedlinePlus defines metabolism as all the physical and chemical processes that convert or use energy, and its examples include breathing, circulating blood, and digesting food. The other lists describe daily activities or states, not the chemical processes themselves.

questionBank.prompt: After a long bike ride, Nia's body repairs her leg muscles, assembling amino acids from her post-ride meal into new muscle protein. In metabolism vocabulary, this repair work is:
options: Catabolism, because large molecules are being split apart for energy
Anabolism, because small building blocks are being built into larger molecules
Digestion, because food is being broken down in the stomach
Excretion, because waste products are leaving the body
questionBank.explanation: Anabolism is the building-and-storing side of metabolism: small building blocks such as amino acids are assembled into larger molecules like muscle protein. Catabolism is the opposite, breaking large molecules down to release energy, and digestion and excretion are related but different processes.
questionBank.skill: Classifying a real repair process as anabolism

questionBank.prompt: Two cousins are the same age, height, and weight, but one lifts weights and has noticeably more muscle. Based on what is known about body composition and metabolic rate, which statement is the most accurate?
options: The cousins burn energy at rest at exactly the same rate because they weigh the same
The less muscular cousin has a higher resting rate because fat conserves energy
The more muscular cousin generally has a higher basal metabolic rate, because muscle burns more energy at rest than fat does
Basal metabolic rate is decided at birth and does not differ between two people
questionBank.explanation: Basal metabolic rate is influenced by body composition: people with more muscle and less fat generally have higher resting rates, because muscle burns more energy at rest than fat. Equal weight alone does not mean equal rates, fat does not raise the resting rate, and BMR is not fixed at birth.
questionBank.skill: Applying body-composition effects to basal metabolic rate

questionBank.prompt: A 70-year-old man notices he feels colder at rest than he did at 25, and his doctor explains that his metabolism has slowed with age. Which explanation matches the scientific picture?
options: Metabolism slows with age partly because muscle mass tends to decrease, and muscle burns more energy at rest than fat does
Metabolism slows with age only because older people happen to eat less
Metabolism speeds up with age because the body works harder to repair aging cells
Metabolism does not change with age; only physical activity changes
questionBank.explanation: Metabolism generally slows as people age, and one reason is that muscle mass tends to decrease with age; since muscle burns more energy at rest than fat, less muscle means a lower resting burn. Eating habits, extra repair work, and 'no change at all' are not the stated causes.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing why resting energy use falls with age

questionBank.prompt: Marco eats a meal of bread, chicken, and butter. After digestion, which statement correctly describes what happens to the nutrients his body absorbs?
options: Only the bread is used by the body; the chicken and butter pass through unused
All three nutrients are converted directly into muscle without any chemical change
The body stores all absorbed nutrients as fat, regardless of which food they came from
The digested forms, sugars from carbohydrates, amino acids from protein, and fatty acids from fat, travel in the blood to cells that use them for energy or store them for later
questionBank.explanation: Digestion breaks carbohydrates into simple sugars such as glucose, proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids; the blood carries these to cells, which use them as energy or store them in tissues such as the liver, muscles, and fat. The other options describe one-food-only use, instant conversion, or blanket storage, none of which matches the process.
questionBank.skill: Tracing digested nutrients to cells as fuel or building blocks

provenance.rightsStatus: Reference-only sources (MedlinePlus/NLM, Nemours KidsHealth, NIDDK/NIH); no source prose adapted — definitions paraphrased, all examples original
provenance.transformation: Definitions and process descriptions from MedlinePlus and Nemours KidsHealth were paraphrased into original EliExplains prose; NIDDK corroborates the scientific framing. All examples (Priya's afternoon, Nia's bike ride, the cousins, the grandfather, Marco's meal) were constructed independently.
